title: Majorana Edge Modes Reshape Kibble-Zurek Scaling in Kitaev Honeycomb Ribbons
authors: Hyesung Choi, Antonio Mandarino, Mahn-Soo Choi
abstract: Recent progress in programmable quantum simulators motivates exact benchmarks for nonequilibrium dynamics in topological quantum matter. We study the Kitaev honeycomb model driven through its critical regions by a linear ramp of the bond coupling $J_z$ over a ramp time $τ$, comparing zigzag and armchair ribbons with fully periodic tubes. The production of excitations exhibits a geometry-dependent finite-size crossover controlled by $N_2/\sqrtτ$, the ratio of the ribbon width to the Kibble--Zurek length. Periodic tubes obey the expected critical-line Kibble--Zurek scaling and serve as the boundary-free benchmark. Zigzag ribbons follow the same scaling until defect production is exponentially suppressed by a finite-width algebraic gap floor associated with the formation of Majorana edge modes, whose occupation is pinned by inversion parity. Armchair ribbons instead support transient Majorana edge modes with exponentially small gaps, producing width-parity-dependent defect plateaus: exactly one defect per unit length for odd widths and an approximate, transient plateau near one half for even widths. The quench-generated entanglement entropy and fermionic logarithmic negativity inherit the same geometry-dependent structure, and the negativity further distinguishes the coherence-borne entanglement of the Kibble--Zurek regime from the population-borne entanglement of the edge-mode plateaus. These results identify boundary Majorana modes as the mechanism controlling departures from ideal Kibble--Zurek dynamics and provide geometry-resolved benchmarks for programmable simulations of topological matter.
summary: This paper analyzes the non-equilibrium dynamics of the Kitaev honeycomb model driven across a topological quantum critical point. By comparing periodic tubes to finite-width ribbons (zigzag and armchair), the authors show that boundary Majorana modes dictate deviations from ideal Kibble-Zurek scaling. This work establishes crucial benchmarks for understanding how edge physics governs topological quantum quenches.
main_problem: The study investigates how the presence of Majorana edge modes on boundaries modifies the universal Kibble-Zurek (KZ) scaling laws observed during non-equilibrium quantum quenches in topological matter.
main_result: Boundary Majorana modes fundamentally alter the dynamics: zigzag ribbons show suppression of defects due to gap flooring, while armchair ribbons exhibit width-parity-dependent defect plateaus, distinguishing them from ideal KZ scaling.
method: The authors analyze the time evolution of the Kitaev honeycomb model by linearly ramping a bond coupling ($J_z$) across a quantum critical point, solving the resulting noninteracting Majorana fermion problem in various geometries.
model_or_system: The system is the Kitaev honeycomb model, analyzed in the flux-free sector, mapped onto noninteracting Majorana fermions. It is studied in cylindrical geometries, comparing fully periodic tubes against finite-width zigzag and armchair ribbons.
key_observables: Defect production density, quench-generated entanglement entropy, and fermionic logarithmic negativity.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system can be treated within the noninteracting Majorana fermion framework and compares results against the expected critical-line Kibble-Zurek scaling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the lattice structure, phase diagram, and finite-size scaling of entanglement entropy and logarithmic negativity for different ribbon geometries (zigzag vs. armchair) compared to periodic tubes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by mapping the spin model to Majorana fermions, then systematically compares the defect scaling and entanglement diagnostics across three boundary conditions (tube, zigzag, armchair) to pinpoint the role of edge modes.
why_interesting: The work provides concrete, geometry-resolved benchmarks for simulating non-equilibrium dynamics in topological systems, directly addressing how boundary physics modifies universal scaling laws relevant to quantum simulation.
